speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fishermen at Port Morien, Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, are in desperate need of improvements to their harbour. The existing facility was constructed over 40 years ago to accommodate 20 small boats and approximately 5,000 lobster traps. Today it accommodates 48 very large vessels and over 10,000 lobster traps. At present, boats have to tie up five to six abreast. All boats use gasoline or diesel fuel, and if a fire should erupt aboard any one of those vessels all the fleet could be lost.
I call upon the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the Minister responsible to provide the necessary money to construct an additional 150-foot extension on the end of the existing wharf, and a 150-foot finger wharf. The request by these fishermen is both reasonable and well thought out. It is time for the Government of Canada to act positively on such a reasonable request.
* v *

Mr. Speaker, for over 300 years dedicated and competent nurses have been serving Canadians. They have played an active and valuable role in the development of our national health care system since the time of Jeanne Mance, the first lay nurse in Canada, during the early years of the 17th century.
The importance of nursing in our health care system is illustrated by the fact that more than 200,000 practising nurses in Canada constitute over 50 per cent of our health care
professionals. Nurses serve the community by caring for all groups of people. Their presence is felt in a variety of venues as they provide care in homes, occupational settings, clinics, hospitals, and in nursing homes.
The nursing profession touches everyone. In recognition of this important contribution I am sure that my colleagues will join me in recognizing National Nurses' Week, and May 12, Florence Nightingale's birthday, International Nurses' Day.

Mr. Speaker, I and my colleagues in the New Democratic Party continue to be profoundly dissatisfied with the manner in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has handled the problems arising out of the eligibility list relating to the Northern Residents Tax Deduction. The Minister of Finance has refused to meet, even at his convenience, with the presidents of the northern Ontario municipal associations or with groups of elected municipal leaders to hear their concerns surrounding the matter.
Unable or unwilling to put forward a solution which will include all northern isolated communities on the eligibility list, the Minister is asking a $2.8 million task force to find the solution. This task force is being given a year and a half to report, which is far too long for communities not on the list to wait.
Six months of staff time was spent to produce the 14 pages of regulations that led to this problem, regulations which anyone with 15 minutes and a map could have determined were going to create divisions. Now we need $2.8 million and 18 months to solve the problem.
Members in this House, too, were led to believe by government Ministers that communities to be added to the list would receive the benefit retroactive to 1987, not 1988 as the press release now states.
Another concern is that the task force proposals are to be essentially revenue neutral. The Minister of Finance must reconsider the mandate of the task force before an already inequitable situation is compounded.

May 10, 1988

Mr. Speaker, this year's round of Order of Canada investitures included three Edmontonians, of whom we are not only very proud but to whom we wish to pay tribute.
Krishan Joshee, Chairman of the Alberta Gaming Commission, is a retired teacher who is widely known for his volunteer work and his dedication to a long list of committees which have fostered multiculturalism in Edmonton and all of Alberta.
Dr. Elenry Kreisel is an author, scholar, teacher, and administrator. A former Vice-President of the University of Alberta he has contributed greatly toward the development of the Eleritage Language Institute.
Mrs. Mary Lobay has, over many years, given most generously of her time to a number of community projects as well as to the University of Alberta, the Edmonton Police Commission, and the Canadian Ukrainian Museum and Archives.
On behalf of Canadians, it is an honour to salute these three distinguished Edmontonians.

subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-CALL FOR MORE RIGID ECONOMIC SANCTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Rev. Allan Boesak, President of the World Alliance of Reformed Churches and the leader of the United Democratic Front, was in Montreal last weekend urging the Canadian Government to act on its promises to impose more rigid economic sanctions on South Africa.
Rev. Boesak warned that the ultra right-wing Conservative Party in South Africa, which is gaining in popularity, and which totally opposes any reform of apartheid, is able to point to the promises made by the Canadian Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Canadian Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) as empty threats that South Africa can ignore without fear of reprisal.
Rev. Boesak also warned that if Canada fails to act on its promise, extremist groups which advocate the use of violence will gain more followers at the cost of moderate groups like the UDF.
When will the Canadian Government act on its promises? As we in the Liberal Party have long stated, mandatory, all-encompassing sanctions must be imposed on South Africa now.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR INCLUSION OF PROPERTY RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the guarantee of property rights is a most important and fundamental right, and one that was neglected by the Liberal Government when drafting the Canadian Charter of Rights.
The sad fact is that, without a guarantee of property rights, the Charter remains a flawed document and a great disappointment to many Canadians.
The recent passage of a Private Member's Motion calling for the inclusion of property rights in the Charter is a clear indication that members of this Government are prepared to offer Canadians such rights, while the NDP, who voted unanimously against the motion, along with 20 per cent of the Liberals, would deny them.
Clearly, the Progressive Conservative Members of the House have reflected the concerns of Canadians through their strong endorsement of property rights. I urge the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to take up this call for action and ensure that property rights are included on the agenda for the next First Ministers' Conference.

subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-ALLEGED NON-ENFORCEMENT OF POLLUTION LAWS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill Andrews of the West Coast Environmental Law Association reports that, according to the federal records, both the federal and provincial Governments are not enforcing pollution laws for British Columbia's 22 pulp mills.
Environment Canada's records show that 21 mills consistently failed to comply with federal limits for one type of pollutant, and 18 mills went over provincial limits for another pollutant.
It would appear that every day last year the 22 mills dumped 2.5 million cu. metres of oxygen-depleting substances and toxic contaminants which end up in the food chain. Yet, Andrews could find no record that either level of government laid charges against even one pulp mill last year in British Columbia for exceeding limits on continuous discharges of pollution.
All this went on under the nose of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) who likes to talk tough on polluters. The Minister should get on top of the situation in British Columbia and across Canada, and start practising what he preaches.

Mr. Speaker, why is it that every time a meeting is scheduled between the native groups and the federal Government a timely leak develops? Whether it involves funding or aboriginal rights, it seems to be too much of a coincidence. Are these leaks happening to ensure that native representatives will be sufficiently angry, thereby guaranteeing failure?
Are these leaks designed to ensure that the process fails and is doomed before native leaders have even met with government officials?
Whenever Indians and Inuit are scheduled to meet with the federal Government, only negative aspects are brought out by the media, so that by the time the leaders sit down at the negotiating table everyone is angry and the whole thing falls apart, with the Indians coming out smoking.

Mr. Speaker, when it comes to our forest industry one thing becomes crystal clear-we must have more value added associated with our timber resource. For years Canadians have said that we must process more of our timber into finished or semi-finished products. Yet more and more raw logs are exported each year.
For example, in 1985 British Columbia exported 2.5 million cubic metres of logs. Last year British Columbia exported 3.4 million cubic metres of logs. This means that we are exporting jobs, since most jobs in the forest industry are associated with timber processing and not with the harvesting of the resource.
It is time we made more of an effort to add value to our Canadian resources. Reducing the volume of raw logs exported would be a major step in the right direction.
I urge the Government to communicate this concern to the Government of British Columbia, and urge it to curtail the export of British Columbia jobs by curtailing the export of raw logs. The sooner the better.

May 10, 1988

VIOLENCE OUTSIDE NEW BRUNSWICK PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVES' ANNUAL MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with this statement I will present you with a resolution that was passed unanimously by the New Brunswick PCs at our annual meeting last Saturday in Moncton, and a newspaper article dated May 7, 1988.
What we witnessed outside was a most disgusting incident involving a handful of disgruntled individuals who felt obliged to make up for their lack of numbers with violence.
Canada is a nation of fairness and tolerance. I think most Canadians do not approve of the actions taken by these protesters. I know that New Brunswickers are not very proud of the shadow which has been cast upon our good character and our warm hospitality.
All political leaders should ask themselves if this kind of behaviour is what we should expect as a sign of things to come in the forthcoming election. I urge all political leaders to denounce this type of violence publicly and to serve notice that it will not be tolerated.

Mr. Speaker, the face of poverty in the country is changing. It is now the face of the child.
I had an opportunity last week to meet with constituents in my riding who are delivering a program in downtown Hamilton, a program on which I served at one time as a member of the board of directors. It has a drop-in centre for the down and out, those disadvantaged in our society who have nowhere else to go.
When I was on the board it served primarily older men, those who had dropped out for a number of reasons. Now, on average, 10 children a day drop into the centre. Four children, on average, under the age of one are brought into the centre. These are children who are part of a situation in which one in five in the country is living in poverty and has nowhere else to go but a drop-in centre. At one time this centre was a haven for the downcast, what we would call the downtrodden, the down and outers. Is this what society has come to?
Unfortunately, our own Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare has refused to study the question of child poverty, even though the cry has been ringing from one end of the country to the other to look at this question in a compassionate way to find solutions so that our children do not have to go to school hungry.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF CANADIAN EXPLORATION INCENTIVE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday, May 3, the Progressive Conservative Government announced the creation of a new Canadian Exploration Incentive Program through the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) and the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew). This new program (CEIP), which will last at least two years, will take effect on January 1, 1989. It provides for federal participation of some $210 million annually to generate private sector investments of around $700 million.
Given the importance of mining exploration for a region like Abitibi-Temiscamingue, this means hundreds of millions of dollars invested in our regional economy for several more years.
What good news for Abitibi-Temiscamingue! Many thanks to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources for this new program!
Once again, it shows how sensitive our Government is to regional economic development and prosperity.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, May 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-103, an Act to increase opportunity for economic development in Atlantic Canada, to establish the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation and to make consequential and related amendments to other Acts, be read the third time and passed.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to debate Bill C-103, an

May 10, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
Act to establish the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. We are at the final stages of this debate and, as New Democrats, we certainly intend to vote in favour of the legislation.
However, I want to qualify that support for the Bill. While we believe this Bill is a step forward, it is not a major step. It falls far short of what one would like to see. We support it because it has the potential to do some good toward diversifying the economy of Atlantic Canada.
When the Economic Council of Canada released its quarterly report in September, 1987 it said that while the overall economy of Canada will expand, one of the challenges we will face is the uneven expansion of that economy. We were forewarned of the continuing boom conditions in certain areas of central Canada where a very high level of prosperity has been generated. However, other parts of Canada have experienced very little growth and, in some cases, no growth at all. While the prosperity in areas of central Canada will continue, the regions of Canada in the Atlantic, the West, and the North will still face economic challenges.
In August, 1987, the Organization of Economic Cooperation and Development released its report. This organization, composed of the 15 wealthiest western nations, studied the western economy and also found that regional disparity was especially noteworthy in Canada. When one considers that geographically Canada is the second largest country in the world, perhaps it is not surprising that we would not experience uniform economic growth and development across the country. However, even this report points out that the Government of Canada would have to face this challenge.
The most recent unemployment figures show that there is a 7.8 per cent unemployment rate in Canada generally, which is a modest decline in the last number of months.
While we are pleased with that downward trend, let me remind the House that the unemployment level in Newfoundland was 17.8 per cent. This suggests that a little over 80 per cent of the people in Newfoundland are employed but included in that number, as many as 50 per cent in some areas, are parttime employees. Many of them are part-time employees because there is no alternative. While they would prefer fulltime employment, they are stuck with part-time work.
Therefore, in real terms, the unemployment rate in Newfoundland is much higher than 17.8 per cent if one takes into account the number of people who are seeking full-time employment.
Newfoundland is one province in Atlantic Canada where regional disparity is most obvious. The difficult economic times continue in spite of the relative prosperity which parts of central Canada are experiencing.
In 1976, the unemployment rate in Newfoundland was 13.4 per cent; increased to 16.8 per cent in 1982; and reached 18.9 per cent in 1983, just before the federal election. In 1984, the year of the federal election, it was over 20 per cent and went up to 21 per cent in 1985. In 1986, the unemployment rate was
20 per cent today and is down to 17.8 per cent. I suggest that it is irrelevant whether the unemployment rate is 17.8 per cent or 20 per cent. It is obviously excessively high.
It has been stated for years that something must be done to address this tragic unemployment situation in Newfoundland. The Government had an opportunity to do something when it decided to establish the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. However, I am afraid that it will fall far short of the objective to remove regional disparity in that area. It will fall far short of creating economic development and business growth in order to employ those thousands of Newfoundlanders and others in Atlantic Canada who are seeking employment.
This becomes most obvious when one considers the financial contribution to ACOA. A minute amount-15 per cent of 1 per cent of the national budget-is being invested into ACOA, which I know you would think unreasonable, Mr. Speaker. It represents $200 million spread over five years, an obvious drop in the bucket.
While this is a small step in the right direction, the financial resources are not available for ACOA to do the job that is necessary.
A particular concern that many Atlantic Canadians expressed to the legislative committee when it travelled in Atlantic Canada was whether this would be new money or money that would normally go into the development of harbours or other economic development initiatives.
We saw in western Canada how money that should have been spent from a soils budget, a fishery budget, or parks budget was coming out of the Western Diversification Office. That is wrong.
Atlantic Canadians are concerned that funds which should come from the fisheries budget, the harbours budget, or another budget will go into the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. They are concerned that it will not be new money but a regurgitation of existing government programs.
I was most amazed to see that the final draft of the legislation for third reading contained no goal to reduce regional disparity, which I thought was its primary objective.
The Government frequently states in the legislation that it may carry out certain initiatives. We need legislation which states that the Government shall support small business, shall support the fishery, shall support the mining sector, and shall support farmers. Governments have an uncanny ability to use the word "may" very creatively. It sounds like it will do something when it has not made the commitment to do so. There is no goal to reduce regional disparity. There is no assurance of equity or fairness among the provinces.
Atlantic Canada is a region comprising several provinces. Is it possible that the Province of Prince Edward Island, for example, could get all or most of the funds from ACOA for one or two years at the expense of other provinces? In terms of
May 10, 1988

our shared jurisdiction and the relationship that the federal Government has with provincial Governments, there ought to have been some inclusion that the funds would be disbursed on an equity basis. In this way every province would know that it is getting its fair share of the financial entitlements associated with this legislation.
I think that we would all agree that $200 million a year over five years is simply not enough. It is inadequate. It is a drop in the bucket. The total budget would be a little over $1 billion. That is simply inadequate when we consider the horrendous challenges that must be overcome to bring down the serious levels of unemployment in Atlantic Canada.
I am very troubled by the fact that Senator Lowell Murray said at the beginning of this process that he would be making the final decisions on who will be receiving the finances. He will be making the final decisions on who will be supported by this legislation. That reeks of political patronage and political favouritism. That is something about which we have to take extraordinary steps to get around. We must get away from the political manipulations of these funds so that the decision making is made on business, economic and industrial terms as opposed to political terms which favour one Party, one person, or one firm over another.
I know that this would shock you, Mr. Speaker, but there is no mention of single industry towns in this legislation. What are we going to do with all the single industry towns that are struggling to survive as their major business phases out or phases down?
What about affordable housing? Is there anything in the legislation which talks about housing? No.
Is a community initiative fund mentioned in the Bill? No. As a matter of fact, infrastructure for communities is eliminated. If you lived in a community, Mr. Speaker, that wanted to develop its industrial infrastructure, better sewage facilities, better water facilities, better streets, better lighting, or better harbours, it could not use this money for those purposes. The one thing that virtually every municipality in the country calls out for is federal government sharing in terms of the development of municipal infrastructure. That is prohibited. Again, it is a real shortcoming.
The Bill does not make much mention at all of a youth initiative fund. As a matter of fact, I can say that it does not make any mention at all of one. The whole matter of the youth of Atlantic Canada is not addressed. This is another serious oversight.
There is nothing in terms of assistance for technological change adjustment. With respect to companies which are modernizing, upgrading, and introducing technological change, there is nothing in the Bill to provide additional funds for training and so on of employees or future workers.
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
Primary industries are overlooked in the Bill. There is no mention of the fishing industry. There is no mention of agriculture. There is no mention of mining. It is rather amazing that forestry and all these other areas were simply left out. These have been some of the major mainstays of Atlantic Canada's economy. To think that we are not introducing special initiatives and special attention concerning them, I find quite amazing.
Obviously environmental clean-up which is a problem in a number of the Atlantic Canadian municipalities was purposefully left out of the Bill-another major oversight.
If the Government really wants to help Atlantic Canada, then we need to have more financial resources available to do so. Perhaps we need to have a rethinking or a rejigging of our monetary policy.
In the newspaper today there is an article with respect to the Bank of Canada's high interest rate policy that is in place to dampen the inflationary fires of pockets of prosperity in central Canada. Goodness knows, there are very few pockets of extreme prosperity in Atlantic Canada that are driving inflation up. Interest rate policy that may be appropriate for the booming and healthy economy of pockets in central Canada act as a retardant in Atlantic Canada by keeping economic development and business development down. In fact, it is very difficult to jack up real business activity there, to kick-start a local economy back into life, with interest rates being as high as they are.
The article states:
While interest rates were intended to take some of the steam out of domestic
spending in Ontario, they have bitten just as hard in provinces like Newfoundland, where there is no steam and unemployment is 17.5 per cent.
This indicates that a shift in monetary policy would do a great deal to help Atlantic Canada.
With respect to government procurement, Governments at the federal, provincial, and local levels could make a combined effort to be procuring more of their goods and services from Atlantic Canadian suppliers. This causes some of us in the Opposition a great deal of concern, because the trade deal signed with the President of the United States will prohibit the Government of Canada from participating in a number of regional development programs and also from having procurement programs just for Atlantic Canada. They will have to be opened up for all of continental North America, which means that the Americans can bid on our government contracts in terms of federal government procurement. Goodness, Mr. Speaker, you will recall that the Americans identified 50 different government programs which they said subsidized the groundfish industry of Atlantic Canada. If that is the attitude of the Americans, then once this trade deal goes into effect and they can identify 50 different programs which they say subsidize the groundfish fishery, it means that we will be slapped with countervails and other retaliatory action.

May 10, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
In closing, I want to say that the legislation is a minor step in the correct direction. There is much to do and a long way to go. I hope we all recognize that this is the first step. Perhaps the next Government of Canada and, more accurately the next New Democratic Party Government of Canada, will be able to follow up very quickly to overcome the shortcomings in today's legislation.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-103 which relates to the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will not do the job of providing economic assistance to Atlantic Canada. It is unfortunate since a great deal has been said about this legislation. A great deal of hope has been created in Atlantic Canada because of it. It was felt that this would be the piece of legislation or the agency that would finally do something about regional disparity in the country.
When we look at all the legislation and the programs that have come forward to try to deal with regional disparity, and when we look at the situation today and find that regional disparity is actually widening, it is incredibly deflating and demoralizing. In a country such as Canada the Government has announced and repeated its wish to reduce regional disparity and then we see what the results are. The results are a widening of regional disparity.
This Bill was based upon a report that the Government commissioned to try to find, through somebody who knew something about regional development, a way to deal with regional disparity, a way to deal with economic difficulties in Atlantic Canada. What the Government did was take the report and change the terms of it that were most important for getting the job done. The report calls for independent directors, people who would be above politics, people who would be interested in the particular application and who would be interested in the project being suggested. Yet what do we have? We have a board of directors that has been appointed and which consists mainly of Progressive Conservative people, those who have been involved in that Party and who have lent support to it.
How are we to get an independent consensus of what a project stands for, if the directors are more interested in passing something that will help people of their own political persuasion? That is not at all in the interests of Atlantic Canada. How will we bring people to Atlantic Canada and have them establish industries in areas that badly need these industries, if we cannot have infrastructure as part of this legislation? There is no allowance for money to be spent on infrastructure. Therefore harbours or services cannot be constructed under this particular legislation. If that cannot be done, we will find that the people, although they are willing to come to Atlantic Canada, will not come unless the services that they want and have every reason to take for granted in other parts of the country are provided in Atlantic Canada.
That is very unfortunate, because services are a very real part of regional development.
The Government seems to be backing away from the concept of regional development. This is seen constantly. For instance, it is seen in the free trade agreement. To the very core the free trade agreement is discouraging and killing the concept of regional development. With the free trade agreement we will be moving to a market economy, which is what the United States wants us to do. If we move to a market economy, we move away from a mixed economy which has been so successful for Canada since the Second World War. The medical programs, the health insurance programs, and the concept of regional development are parts of the fibre of that program, but, the Government wants to back away from that.
The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) has asked what will we do about one-industry towns. There are 800 one-industry towns in Canada. Without the concept of regional development and aiding those industries that need assistance to make them viable, providing that they can be viable, we will lose not only the industries but the towns.
The Government believes that the private sector can do it. That is not the case. The private sector is not doing it. A good example is a recent Small Businesses Loans Act report for the 12-month period ended March 31, 1987. This report was issued a few weeks ago in April. Not only do we have a report which shows that the Government's programs are not working, but the Government cannot get the report out until more than a year after the end of the period dealt with in the particular report.
In the report it shows that the Small Businesses Loans Act, which gives government support to the lending institutions to guarantee that losses under these loans will be a certain small percentage, is not assisting the areas that need it most. The 85 per cent guarantee the federal Government puts on moneys lent by the chartered banks of Canada is not going to the customers who really need this assistance. If we look in the report we will see that the four Atlantic provinces together only receive 6 per cent of the money allocated under the Small Businesses Loans Act. That is a travesty. One cannot say that the private sector will do the job of correcting regional disparity, and then allow the banks to provide these loans to their privileged customers and not to the people who need this assistance. The idea of that program was to guarantee the major part of a loan to those who would not ordinarily qualify because they were somewhat of a risk. It turns out that the loans are not going to these companies or these people at all.
An interesting aspect of Bill C-103 is that the first part deals with the establishment of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. The second part deals with the Cape Breton Development Corporation. This Bill deals with two entirely separate things. It also deals with the Government's intention to do away with the industrial development division of the Cape Breton Development Corporation and to establish a new
May 10, 1988

Crown corporation which will be called Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation.
The Government has also brought forward Bill C-127 which deals with the Cape Breton Development Corporation. It increases the allotment of the coal division of the Cape Breton Development Corporation from $25 million to $50 million. That is where the part dealing with the industrial development division should be. In the Cape Breton Development Corporation there are two divisions-the coal division, which is dealt with in Bill C-127, and the industrial development division, which is the second part of the Bill being discussed today. There should have been one Bill dealing with the Cape Breton Development Corporation, Bill C-127. The Government wants to do away with the industrial development division.
The Cape Breton Development Corporation Act was first passed in 1967 under the then Government of Prime Minister Lester Pearson. At that particular time it was deemed that the economy of Cape Breton was in such a state of deterioration that a special piece of legislation had to be brought forward to deal with this very serious question. A Bill was put forward that had two parts, one dealing with the coal division and the second one promoting industrial development through the industrial development division, a second division of that corporation.
If in 1967 the Government of Canada felt that the situation was so serious that this Act was necessary, what business has the Government today in dismantling the industrial development division? The economic situation in Cape Breton is worse now than it was 21 years ago. At that time there were heavy water plants. This Government said that they would not be closed until alternate employment was found for the workers, but it closed them anyway without any alternate employment. There is a steel plant employing only 50 per cent of the workers that it was employing 21 years ago. There is a mining industry that has had a substantial reduction, with at least a thousand people less today than in 1967. Because of the downturn in the economy, industries and offices located in industrial Cape Breton have left and consolidated in other centres in Atlantic Canada, thereby losing very valuable jobs, good paying jobs, and adding tremendously to the problems in that area.
The Government is now saying: "Let us get rid of the industrial development division; the people in 1967 did not know what they were talking about". They knew what they were talking about; it was an excellent piece of legislation. The industrial development division is an excellent facility and is much needed in Cape Breton Island.
Once the industrial development division under DEVCO is done away with, there will be only one division-the coal division. That will make Cape Breton Development Corporation an ideal candidate in the mind of the Government for privatization. That seems to be what the Government has in mind. It is not the welfare of the people of Cape Breton that is
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
most important; it is facilitating the game plan of the Government. People do not matter. The Government has a little chart and it wants to ping off Crown corporations, regardless of what that indiscriminate selling off will do to the people who will be most affected by those sales.
By doing away with the industrial development division, there is only one division, the coal division, which will easily allow the Government to fulfil its dream of privatizing the Cape Breton Development Corporation. The problem in doing away with the industrial development division is that it is also greatly hampering the chances of Cape Breton to have a meaningful economic revival. The industrial development division had a budget that was given to DEVCO and that it could use for the betterment of Cape Breton Island. It has been successful. I would say that it has not been as successful as it should have been, because it has not been used as well as it could have been.
The facility is there, the vehicle is there, and the ability of this division to add greatly to the industrial and economic benefit of industrial Cape Breton exists today as much and perhaps more than it has in the past. By doing away with that division we do away with this budget. The Government is saying not to worry about the loss of the industrial development division in Cape Breton, because it is setting up a whole new Crown corporation which will be called Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. It already has an agency in Cape Breton called Enterprise Cape Breton. Now it is to set up another corporation called Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation.
Not only does the Government have no idea how to deal with questions of regional disparity, but it has absolutely no imagination. It will have one agency called Enterprise Cape Breton and a second one called Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. One would not doubt that the Government is very dull, but it is hard to believe that its dullness has allowed it to make such an unimaginative move as to name one corporation almost exactly the same as an existing agency. What it really intends to do, of course, is to have a corporation called Enterprise Cape Breton and another one called Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation so that it can merge the two without anyone really noticing. No one will ever know which is which because they both have the same name. It is absolutely ludicrous.
However, this stance taken by the Government has a purpose, that is, to do away with one of the agencies gradually without anyone noticing it is gone. Of course the two agencies with practically the same name will both be under the umbrella of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. Although this is a separate Crown corporation which the Government is proposing, Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation, the president of the corporation will be the same president as the president of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities

May 10, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
Agency. It is economically incestuous. It is absolutely incredible that the Government would actually try to pass this off on the people this country.
What we will have is two agencies with the same name, the same president, under the same umbrella, and ultimately reporting through a diverse and devious means to the same board of directors. What we will really have is the same agency. The Government is trying to tell us that these are two different agencies. That is like saying that when you get change for a quarter you have three times as much money because you have two dimes and a nickel. That is the extent of the ridiculous position the Government is trying to pass off on the people of Cape Breton, and it will not work.
The people of Cape Breton will not accept, yet again, another kick in the teeth by this Government. It has been one thing after another. Every time the Government makes a move, we find that what it has given back is only part of what it has taken away, if in fact it gives anything back. This has to stop. It is evident now,-and it will become more evident as we go along if this Bill is passed-that other Departments will gradually cut back their spending. They will point to the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and tell us that they do not have to spend on small craft harbours, transportation, or other departmental expenditures on structures and institutions which increase much needed employment in these areas. They will not provide the tremendously important services which are necessary if we are to have economic development.
Although there are some good features in this Bill, the good features will be completely nullified by the sleight of hand of the Government in the actual operation. The people of Cape Breton suffer most of all because they will not have the industrial development division; it is to be taken away from them. They will be left with just a piece of an agency, they already have in two separate parts.
I would ask the Government to delete any reference to the Cape Breton Development Corporation, to delete Clauses Nos. 25 to 52 dealing with the Cape Breton Development Corporation, and to make important and meaningful changes to the rest of the Bill so that it will in fact be of benefit to the people of Atlantic Canada instead of the sleight of hand it is right now.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to prolong debate, but I would like to make a few comments with regard to the Hon. Member's speech. He made a number of suggestions, and perhaps innuendoes with respect to the board and how it is constituted. Everyone knows the board is appointed by the Minister responsible. The existing 19-member board was appointed in consultation with the provinces. When we look at the list of board members, we note they represent provincial Governments. I believe there is someone from the cabinet secretariat of both the Province of Newfoundland and the Province of New Brunswick. It would be very difficult for us merely to choose from among our friends, as the Member
has indicated, people who would pass or approve projects according to who they were.
One of the debates in Atlantic Canada when the committee held its hearings was on whether or not the board should have decision-making ability. The Government, in the way it set the board up and since then in the speeches of the Minister responsible and in the deliberations of the committee, agreed that the board should not have decision-making power. Therefore it is impossible for the board to make a decision on whether application a or application b will be accepted. That is done through the bureaucracy; the board is there to set policy. I, for one, as a Member from Atlantic Canada did not want to see a board that could actually make decisions with regard to applications. That would be too much like the political influence to which the Hon. Member made reference, and we have avoided it. This board is not making decisions on applications. It is there to provide policy and direction and guidance to the Minister based upon its work experience in Atlantic Canada.
I can tell the Hon. Member as a Member from Moncton that when I looked at the list of members of the board I saw a name I did not recognize. I can assure him that I have no idea of that individual's political inclination, nor did I have any input into that actual nomination. In fact, it may have come almost strictly from bureaucrats. I see that at one time he was an employee of DRIE in Atlantic Canada. He then realized, perhaps, the errors of his ways, recognizing there was an opportunity to make a fair amount of money in the manufacturing industry of Atlantic Canada. He is now a successful entrepreneur, operating a small business which is very rapidly growing into a large business in the Dieppe area of my constituency.
I think the suggestions with respect to the board and its influence are misleading. We all recognize that anyone appointed by a politician is obviously open to the question of their political leanings. I think in this case that the Minister and the Government made every effort, in consultation with their colleagues and counterparts in the provinces, to ensure that we set up a board which would have a great deal of credibility, as well as a lot of expertise.
The Member talked about infrastructure. It is true that this program is not designed to solve the problems of Halifax Harbour. He should realize as a Member from Cape Breton- and I can tell him that as the Member for Moncton-that with only $1.05 billion we cannot afford in any one year to give $206 million to Halifax. That is a matter that can best be addressed by the Province of Nova Scotia negotiating an ERDA agreement with the Government of Canada through ACOA and its Minister responsible. That is the best way to handle infrastructure problems in Atlantic Canada.
This particular piece of legislation provides infrastructure for specific site problems. If there is a situation where an industry can start, if there is infrastructure development to take place leading to that site, there is an option under this
May 10, 1988

legislation for the Minister to act. Those are two areas I wanted to clarify with regard to third reading. I appreciate the points of concern the Member has brought to our attention, and I trust that he understands the explanation I have given.

Mr. Speaker, I can appreciate the point of view of the Member for Moncton (Mr. Cochrane) although I do disagree. I feel there is a great deal of political intervention in the appointment of these directors.
It was initially stated that when this agency was to be set up the decision was to be made in Atlantic Canada. The main objection in Atlantic Canada was that you could have approval locally but you sent the projects to Ottawa for internal review in the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion which either delayed them until the projects were not feasible any more or just turned them down. It was believed that by getting perhaps a little more objective support for what was necessary-perhaps a feeling for the needs of the people in the region of Atlantic Canada-that more of the viable projects would be approved. As the Hon. Member for Moncton has said, the Government has scuttled that. We are back to the old ways of doing things, of sending them back to Ottawa; let Ottawa sit on them and ignore the situation in the areas that really need assistance.
What the Government is proposing is a step backward and we cannot afford that. We have to move ahead. We must narrow the gap in regional disparity, not widen it as this Bill will do. With respect to infrastructure, we are not talking about a major program such as Halifax Harbour. I made no mention of Halifax Harbour. That is a subsidiary agreement between the province and the federal Government. What we need are projects not directly related to one particular industry but ones that will have an over-all effect in areas which are really in serious economic difficulty. This piece of legislation does not address that need.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is ironic that we should have this debate today, coming as it does on the heels of the debate yesterday which I think was far more revealing, namely, the dispute between Canada and France over fish. It seems to me that was far more revealing about the intentions and the attitude of the Government. What disturbed me in the debate yesterday when we talked about Atlantic opportunities were the comments of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), and I believe he made the same comments on Friday. I refer to yesterday's Hansard. In response to a question from me on whether he would take firm action and
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
get tough with France, whether he would do something tangible, whether he would do something realistic to bring this matter to a head and show the Government of France that we were not happy with the kind of treatment that our fishermen were getting, he said:
I think one knows that a trade war which might begin with this kind of issue would go on to something else. One of the things it might go on to, 1 say to those who are interested in the economy of Atlantic Canada, for example, might be the investment in Michelin Tire.
If there is a trade war, among the casualties in Canada of this trade war the Liberals are trying to start gratuitously, might be a thousand employees of Michelin Tire in Nova Scotia. The Liberal Party might want casually to throw those Canadians out of work.
How silly, Mr. Speaker. When the head of Michelin Tire in Canada heard those remarks, he said: "Oh, my goodness". Then he consulted his lawyer and said: "We are in business. We are not going to deal with that kind of statement". Do we think for a minute the Government of France has any way of pulling Michelin Tire out of Nova Scotia? Does anyone seriously think that that is possible? Michelin Tire is in business to make money like any other business. Making money comes first with any business. It is silly to say that the Government of France will somehow force Michelin Tire out of Nova Scotia. It is okay for the Minister to try to protect jobs that already exist in other parts of Canada, but when it comes to jobs in a province like Newfoundland which is totally dependent on the fishery, fish mean jobs for us; if we do not have access to fish we do not have jobs. It is all very well for the Government to say to one part of Canada, "we are very interested in protecting your jobs and therefore we are not going to start a trade war with France but those jobs in Newfoundland, those jobs of the fishermen, are expendable."
We are hostages, Mr. Speaker. The question becomes: Are we real Canadians or not? Are we equal Canadians? Do we have equal opportunity? The answer that we happen to come to is no. We do not have equal opportunity. Moreover, it is very apparent that we do not have any influence or clout with the Government of Canada. The seven seats we hold in this Parliament are not enough to give us the kind of access to equality that we need if we are to survive.
Fish is what we are all about. We are an island. We fish. That is what we came for in the first place. If our fishermen do not have access to fish, they do not have jobs. If they have to get permits from the Government of France before they go fishing, what is this country coming to? I ask again: Are we Canadians or are we not? Do we have a government that is prepared to stand up and fight for us? What Government should we refer to? Should we go to the French Government? Should we go to the French Parliament and put our case there? I want to see this Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency in that context. We do not want a billion dollars. What we want is fish. The Government of Canada is saying, like Marie Antoinette: "Let them eat cake". It is saying: "Do you want fish? No, you cannot have fish. You can have a billion dollars. Take a billion dollars. Let them eat cake". That is what we are getting from the Government, and it disturbs me

May 10, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
as a representative of Newfoundland in this Parliament that that can be said and that we have to be hostages in that way.
Canadianism means more to us than that. Canada means more to us than that. When we voted, only by 52 per cent in 1949, not that long ago, we thought that we were getting into a country where we would be equal partners and that we would have a country which would stand up and fight for us. That is what we are asking the Government to do for us. We are not asking for a billion dollars. We do not want money. We do not want hand-outs. We want the possibility to make it on our own. That means access to fish.
This is the same Government when talking about opportunity to fish that said "no" to the Labrador shrimp company on the Labrador coast which asked for a quota of northern cod. It said: "You may live next to that resource. You may have fished it for a very long time. You may depend on it for a livelihood, but you cannot have a quota of offshore cod. There are other Canadian firms that can have it. The European Common Market can have it but you", the Labrador shrimp company, "cannot have access to that northern cod". As a result of that attitude, in the community of Cartwright which is not very big, maybe made up of 500 people, 80 people have jobs in the fish plant, but that plant will be closed this summer. It will be open for the salmon season, which is a few weeks. The fishermen will make a few dollars, but then the plant will be closed down because the fishermen will not have access to a supply of northern cod. That is the kind of policy in existence, and we are talking about Atlantic Canada opportunities. I say again: "Who wants a hand-out?" What people want is access to fish. That is what gives us economic survival. That is what we have been told by the Government that we cannot have.
I have other problems with this Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. As I said before in the House-and I want to say it again today-the problem is that the money has to be spent on business. We heard the Hon. Member for Moncton (Mr. Cochrane) point out that we can have infrastructure if it is project-related. We have a lot of needs in Atlantic Canada that are not project-related. We have a lot of roads that need building. We have a lot of water systems that need putting in place.
Those things have to be there if we are to provide a climate in which business can survive. No business will go into a community that does not have a water system, a paved road, three-phase power or the kind of infrastructure in which business can survive. It is meaningless to come up with $1 billion to encourage businesses to set up if we do not put the infrastructure in place first.
Donald Savoie, the man the Government appointed, said much the same thing. He referred as a model to the original agency that was set up for Atlantic Canada, the Atlantic Development Board. Mr. Savoie was quoted in Atlantic Insight as saying that a return to a more grass roots, selfsustaining approach would be the better alternative. The article reads:
Savoie used the old Atlantic Development Board (ADB) as a model for his new federal agency. Created in the early 1960's-
-created by a Conservative Government, a Government which at that time had some imagination and foresight:
-the ADB was given six years to spend $150 million to improve the infrastructure of the region. During this period the area's highways were paved, hydro plants were built and much needed information on the Atlantic Economy was collected-
The article in Atlantic Insight goes on to say:
The board's last president, Ian MacKeigan, the 72-year-old former Chief Justice of the Nova Scotia Supreme Court, remains convinced that the ADB, with its local board of directors and less ambitious mandate, was a very better approach to regional development-
Then we moved on to DREE, and we saw the same kind of flexibility to respond to the real needs of Canadians, the flexibility which is missing in this particular proposal.
Even what is in place now is causing us difficulties. There is still the same old red tape. I was in Goose Bay last week, and a man who owns a laundry, George Shepherd, came to me and said: "I want to build a new laundry. The economy in Goose Bay is good now, business is booming. I want to spend $300,000, I will create 12 jobs and I want money from the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency".
Do you know what they said to him? They said: "You can't get any money because you are a retail outlet". They said this to the man who is the only such operator in a community of
8,000	people. He has contracts with the Armed Forces and with the German Air Force. Queen Beatrix spoke to us this morning. He has a contract to service the Dutch Air Force in Goose Bay. He services the Marine Atlantic and the coastal boats. He operates a service industry, not a retail industry. Yet the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is telling this man that he cannot qualify because he is in the retail business. That kind of inflexibility has to stop if we are to make any progress at all and if this is to do any good at all. Otherwise the $1 billion will be useless, or if it is not useless, it will certainly not come to us. This has to be changed as well.
We are told that the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will somehow get into training. The North Warning System is being constructed in northern Canada and there are several sites in Labrador. Maybe 5 per cent of those employed at some of those sites are local people. In the long term, the same percentage will hold. This is because local people do not have the skills.
Many of the people who live in those communities are native people. Do you know what the Government has just done, Mr. Speaker? The Government has just cut back on the amount of funds available for post-secondary education for native people. The North Warning System is an initiative of the Government of Canada, and I applaud the Government for it. It is a good idea and it needs to be done. There is 100 per cent support for that. However, the Government has also cut back on the
May 10, 1988

amount of training funds that will be available for postsecondary education for native people. The Government cannot have it both ways. It cannot say that it wants local and native people to be employed by the North Warning System and then cut off the training funds. If these people do not have training, they will not get the jobs.
What will the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency do about that? Will it solve that problem? That is an Atlantic Canadian problem, a training problem and an economic problem. I do not see any evidence that the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is doing much about that at this time.
The last point I want to make deals with opportunities in Atlantic Canada. In Labrador, there are 10,000 megawatts of electricity flowing to the sea every day, untapped. There are all sorts of markets for that in the United States. There is a lot of potential there. There are even potential markets in other parts of eastern Canada. However, as a result of a combination of the free trade agreement and the deregulation policy of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse), it is less likely now that producing provinces will have to consult with the Atlantic Provinces before they develop their hydro resources.
When Quebec developed a hydro resource for sale to the U.S. in the past, it had to go to other provinces and ask if they wanted the power. The province was forced to go to the National Energy Board to get clearance. There was a mechanism to see that the Atlantic Provinces could take advantage of and buy that power. That mechanism no longer exists.
I make this point because in 1992, in a province which has
10,000	untapped megawatts of electricity flowing to the sea every day, we will run out of power. What supports business and industry? What it is that makes it go? What is the juice, the blood that runs through the veins of business and industry? It is power, and if we do not have that, what can we do? What will our future be like?
In this debate on the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, we must look at development in context. We must look at it in the context of the free trade agreement and in the context of the deregulation policy of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who says that anybody anywhere can sell anything to the United States at any time for whatever price he can get, and he does not have to make any deals with Atlantic Canada or ask Atlantic Canadians if they want to participate and develop hydro resources together. That is the reality.
I hope that the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will work. I must say that not too many other approaches have. Although we have caught up in relation to where we were in the past, we are still, in relative terms, far behind, too far behind, the rest of Canada. I hope that the agency will work, but it will not work unless the items I have identified are dealt with and are solved.
