speechtext: Order, please. Pursuant to Standing Order 13(4)(a), I have been requested by the Chief Government Whip to defer the division until today at a later time. Accordingly, the division on the question now before the House stands deferred until after Private Members' Business later this day, at which time the bells to call in the Members will be sounded for not more than 15 minutes.

The House resumed from Tuesday, May 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-113, an Act to promote the development and diversification of the economy of western Canada, to establish the Department of Western Economic Diversification and to make consequential amendments to other Acts, be read the third time and passed, and the motion of Mr. Hawkes:

May 10, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
That this question be now put.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to make a few remarks on Bill C-113 and the Department of Western Economic Diversification. I want to stress the importance of this issue to western Canada. Certainly we can see that importance when we look at the continuing high unemployment figures, particularly in British Columbia where they have been in double digits almost continuously for the last five years. We are very concerned that the trade agreement reached between the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and President Reagan is going to confirm that kind of high unemployment. The Tories say that agreement is going to open up new opportunities for western Canada. In fact, it will confirm western Canada in its present role of hewers of wood and drawers of water. Unfortunately, while we are hewing more wood and drawing more water, there are fewer people doing it.
I want to look at some figures just produced by the Council of Forest Industries of British Columbia. They talk about the number of jobs in B.C. in the forest industry between 1978 and 1985. In 1978 the logging industry employed 23,168 people. In 1985 it was 19,488, or a loss of 4,000. In the wood industry there were 50,955 jobs in 1978. In 1985 there were 39,603, or a loss of more than 10,000. In pulp and paper there were 20,655 jobs in 1978, and in 1985 this had dropped to 16,850, or a loss of 4,000 jobs. The total in all those industries in 1978 was 94,778 jobs. By 1985 that had dropped to 75,941, or a loss of 20,000. Yet at the same time production went up.
In 1978 in the coast forest region we produced 32,338 thousand cubic metres of log production. In 1987 it had increased to 33,791 thousand cubic metres. In the interior forest region it was 42,815 thousand cubic metres in 1978, and 56,800 thousand cubic metres in 1987. The total for all of British Columbia in 1978 was 75,153 thousand cubic metres. That increased in 1987 to 90,591 thousand cubic metres. At the same time as we lost 20,000 jobs we are producing more wood than ever before.
Unfortunately, we are not processing that wood in British Columbia or even in Canada. We are exporting it. In 1978 we exported 585,500 cubic metres. By 1987 that had risen to 3,394,900 cubic metres. In other words, we were exporting six times as much in 1987 as we were in 1978. We are producing more, exporting more, and yet we have fewer employees. The trade deal is going to make that situation worse.
We can see the urgent need for some kind of redress when we look at the question of federal procurement in western Canada. Again the situation is getting worse. Certainly members of the Conservative Party in 1981 would not have been very happy that only 15.5 per cent of federal procurement came from western Canada. In 1984-85, when the Government came to office, it had dropped to 13.9 per cent. Yet in 1986-87 it dropped again to 11.5 per cent. It has continued to decline whether under a Liberal Government or Conservative Government. It dropped from an already poor figure in 1981-82, to a
disastrous figure where the four western provinces are getting only 11.5 per cent of federal procurement.
British Columbia, as you know, has 11.4 per cent of Canada's total population, yet that province, combined with Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, only gets 11.5 per cent of federal procurement. British Columbia itself gets only 3.6 per cent of federal procurement for its 11.4 per cent of the population. Compare that with Ontario and Quebec which together get 76 per cent of federal procurement. We have nothing against Ontario and Quebec, we would simply like to have our share. We are concerned that this Bill does not address that kind of systemic inequity directed toward western Canada and which, I might point out with reference to the Bill just passed, is also shared by Atlantic Canada.
We are concerned that the whole western diversification initiative is not part of a co-ordinated government plan which will see diversification and regional development take place in western Canada. For example, we can look at an editorial in today's Toronto Star which points out that the Bank of Canada's high interest rate policy is adversely affecting regions outside of central Canada. The article says that in his crusade to slow the Ontario economy, Bank of Canada Governor John Crow has asked the rest of Canada to pay an inordinate price. In March and April the other nine provinces together lost 7,000 jobs.
The Bank of Canada and the Government are concerned that perhaps the economy of southern Ontario is superheated so they want to cool it off a little bit. In doing so by raising interest rates and the value of the dollar, they are cooling off an economy which has been on ice for the last several years, the economy of western Canada and eastern Canada. We in British Columbia do not need to have our economy cooled off. We do not need high interest rates to prevent the boom from getting out of hand because we have not seen the boom. We are still trying to recover from the recession of 1982, 1983, 1984, 1985, 1986 and 1987. It is now 1988 and we are still facing some very difficult times.
There are people in my constituency who were laid off five years ago and still have not found work. Young people used to be able to expect that they would find work on Vancouver Island or elsewhere in British Columbia when they grew up. They are now having to come to Toronto to find work. We have policies geared toward central Canada which do not deal with the very real concerns in western Canada. Bill C-113 and the whole western diversification initiative does not begin to deal with that issue.
Raising the value of the Canadian dollar vis-a-vis the American dollar will make it much more difficult for our exports to compete in the American market. All the Government's very optimistic projections in terms of the trade agreement with the United States were premised on a 73 cent or 74 cent Canadian dollar. Now that it is up to 81 cents our
May 10, 1988

products are much less competitive and the trade deal will definitely result in job losses for Canadians.
We are concerned that while the goal of Bill C-l 13, western diversification, is good, the commitment of the Government and the provisions of the Bill do not reach toward that goal in any significant way. For example, the Government has committed $1.2 billion over five years to this fund. That works out to something like $60 million on an average for each of the four western provinces per year. Considering the massive problems and the need out there, this will be no more than a drop in the bucket.
I want to emphasize that my concerns on this issue are not simply partisan. We see in the submission of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business to the committee that these concerns are shared by many people across Canada. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business could not be accused of supporting the New Democratic Party as a general rule. It is not a group of closet socialists or anything. Their "Executive Summary" reads in part as follows:
Yet our enthusiasm has been tempered by growing concern that the Western Diversification initiative is degenerating into at least one or all of the following:
-a political slush fund to support vulnerable constituencies, lure in big business or bail out obsolete industries in hopes of getting short-term political profile
-a bureaucratic slush fund available for other line departments and Ministers to raid in lieu of other national programs that should have their fair share spent in the West
-a narrow and highly centralized approach to diversification with continued emphasis on megaprojects or traditional resource extraction and development
-a confusing "black box" lacking clear criteria or policy direction, and on a collision course with a myriad of client groups who are inevitably going to see thousands of applications rejected and thousands of hopes dashed.
In other words, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business is very concerned that the Western Diversification Fund seems to be very unfocused, seems to be at the mercy of Departments which can raid it, and seems to be something that can be used for partisan political advantage. It is arousing all kinds of hopes but there is very little chance that the majority of those hopes will be fulfilled.
In exchange for this the Canadian Federation of Independent Business suggests that there should be a specific focus on the small business sector. It is important that we recognize the importance of the small business sector in this House, not only with our speeches but in the legislation that we pass. As the Federation points out in its brief, job growth in the past few years in western Canada has been almost exclusively from the small business sector.
In Manitoba in 1985, 64 per cent of new jobs were created by small business. In Alberta 66 per cent of new jobs were created by small business, that is businesses with less than 20 employees. In Saskatchewan 76 per cent of new jobs were created by small business, and in British Columbia the figure was over 100 per cent because big business, companies with
Western Economic Diversification Act
more than 500 employees, lost 6 per cent of the jobs they previously had.
It is, therefore, important that we recognize the entrepreneurial spirit in ways which will help it to develop. It is not enough to say that small business and entrepreneurs will find a way to develop. One of the roles of government is to create the structures, the infrastructure, and the processes which will enable that small business spirit to take root.
If you look at the record of New Democratic Party Governments in Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and British Columbia, you will see that while we are sometimes accused of being overcentralist and everything else, in fact the initiatives which we have brought in have helped small business much more than some of the initiatives of the so-called free enterprise Parties. We need to find ways to help that spirit find outlets in ventures which have a reasonable chance of success.
The Canadian Federation of Independent Business suggests four major areas of activity, the first being community development. It is good to see that the Canadian Federation of Independent Business recognizes that development takes place in the community, that it is not simply a matter of the lone entrepreneur going out by herself or himself against a hostile world.
Therefore, the Federation suggests the following four major areas of activity:
1.	community development, whether it be seed capital for establishment of local business advisory networks and economic planning at the local level, or through financing of sectoral trade associations to assist with market research and information
2.	risk financing and equity investment in small business, through use of various regional tax incentives or W.D.O.-backed loan guarantees
3.	promotion and support of a western entrepreneurial culture
4.	advocacy throughout all federal agencies on behalf of the West.
These are some of the things we would like to see happening. I would particularly like to emphasize the role of women entrepreneurs because a great many of the new businesses which have been started in the last number of years, up to 65 per cent, have been started by women. In fact, new businesses started by women have a much higher rate of success than businesses started by men. Yet, very often, these are the very businesses which need help. That is a special need which should be recognized in this legislation.
Unfortunately, with regard to the funds being spent there seems to be a continued over-emphasis by the Government on megaprojects. We have seen no clear plan for spending the $1.2 billion in the Western Diversification Fund. For example, there was a commitment of millions of dollars to the Salmonid Enhancement fund in British Columbia. We all admit that that money was badly needed. However, it should have come from the regular A-based budget of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. Instead, it came from the Western Diversification Fund which gives point to the criticism I read earlier of the Federation of Independent Business that that

May 10, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
fund can be used as a slush fund for bureaucrats from other Departments which will raid it to get money for their projects.
That money should have come from the regular budget of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. It is part of the Government's commitment to British Columbia, part of an ongoing commitment. To say that it is part of a new western diversification initiative is sheer nonsense and poppycock. The Prime Minister promised that the money for the western diversification initiative will be new money. It seems to me that it should have been new money for the Department of Fisheries and Oceans.
There was a commitment of $418,000 from the Western Diversification Fund for the BF Goodrich plant. There are no new jobs in that. There is $9.5 million to the second largest pulp and paper complex in Japan in order to establish a huge complex in northern Alberta. Surely large operations like that should be able to generate their own capital either internally or through bank loans. Why is an already limited Western Diversification Fund being frittered away in situations like this?
Let me refer again to the concerns that were raised by Mr. Dennis Young, President of the Canadian Association of Single Industry Towns, when he appeared before the committee. He pointed out that over 400 single industry towns have disappeared from Canada in the last 100 years. Certainly, many of those single industry towns that have disappeared were in western Canada. Yet the Bill does nothing to recognize the need to build on community strengths of single industry towns and help them diversify. There is nothing in the Bill that specifically guarantees that there can be help for community development, and for community infrastructure.
Mr. Young pointed to the need for a bottom-up approach to development. He pointed to the need for western initiatives to work with local communities for the kind of development that will be in line with what the communities as a whole want, rather than selectively choosing projects and approving them on a proposal by proposal basis.
Finally, I want to refer to some of the proposals that the New Democratic Party has made. We want a $1.2 billion annual fund for community infrastructure all across Canada. However, this would particularly help western Canada. We propose a $200 million annual fund for diversification of single industry towns; $500 million for affordable housing and to perhaps work on overcoming that backlog in native Indian communities to which we have referred. We propose funding for community initiatives and youth initiatives; funds to help people cope with the problems of technological change.
In conclusion, we do not oppose this Bill but certainly have no confidence that it will be able to do the very important job for western Canada that we believe needs to be done.
Mr. Speaker, I have had some further thought on this Bill-

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Watch out.

-which I know my hon. friends opposite will be anxious to hear. I was in Saskatchewan last weekend and talked to many people. I deliberately raised the question of western diversification and three or four farmers to whom I spoke told me that it had been tried before. That is what I told the House earlier when I spoke to this Bill. When one looks at the history of western Canada, one can see that we have been through this scheme three or four times. Furthermore, they do not believe in this program. In fact, their disbelief is such that they even nominated me to run again in the next election. If they had believed in this program, they would not have bothered.
No matter what political party is in power, it must answer the question: Diversify to what? There must be a national industrial strategy which involves governments at all levels, the private sector, agriculture, the fishery, forestry, and the trade union movement. That is what has been done in West Germany, Holland, Sweden and Norway for the last 30 years. Such a strategy sets out a plan for the economy through consultation. The largest corporations in Canada plan their activities for the next 20 years. Yet governments in the last 40 years have devised temporary, ad hoc programs.
My hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Mala-hat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) referred to the comments of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. That is hardly a group that can be referred to as wild-eyed socialists. They referred to this Western Diversification Program as nothing more than a narrow, short-sighted operation. Government Members who were here during the days of Otto Lang will recall speeches about political slush funds. That is what the Canadian Federation of Independent Business calls this fund. It is a highly centralized bureaucratic operation which creates the potential of conflict between Departments. The Bill does not give the Minister the authority he requires to deal effectively with other Departments.
I repeat that there must be a goal for diversification. There must be an industrial strategy that takes into account our geography, our climate and the distance over which we must move goods that are processed and manufactured in the regions of Canada. There should be a mechanism to equalize transportation costs so that they are a relatively neutral factor and would allow processors and manufacturers throughout Canada to deliver their goods to the market with an equal chance to compete.
The competition should be on quality and quantity of product, capability of delivery, warranties, salesmanship, advertising, all the things that go into selling something that someone is producing, manufacturing or processing. This Bill does nothing to attack a problem that we have always had in
May 10, 1988

western and Atlantic Canada. We discriminate against people because of where they happen to live and where they happen to produce their goods. Therefore, this legislation cannot accomplish what the Government wants it to do, something which we all agree should be done.
There is a classic case in western Canada and Atlantic Canada where the so-called free market forces do not work. I say that because entrepreneurs in western and Atlantic Canada are disadvantaged. They do not have a full and fair chance under the classic free market forces because of where they are located. The deck is stacked against them right off the bat.
Let me illustrate my point, Mr. Speaker. In the late 1940s and the early 1950s we got into the growing of rapeseed, which is now called Canola. We established up to a dozen oilseed processing plants in the three prairie provinces. They were doing pretty good. They were gradually building up and establishing a market in central Canada, the United States and overseas. However, there was a problem with respect to the cost of moving it. There was a famous court case which dealt with the problem. It occurred when Mr. Diefenbaker was Prime Minister of Canada. Rapeseed was finally established as a grain, which took a lot of doing. Rapeseed products then became grain products. Thus by the late 1960s there were oilseed crushing plants going in all three prairie provinces. I think there were one or two in or near your city, too, Mr. Speaker.
What happened then? The next thing we know the Americans got great subsidies on soybeans, corn and cotton seed, as well as palmseed oil. They were putting stuff into Canada in the name of free trade. Our processors in western Canada were faced with transportation costs just to get their product to Ontario, not to mention the United States or overseas. To add insult to injury, this occurred when the Government of the day did not have an industrial strategy. What did they do? It gave, I believe it was, $6 million in grants to build an oilseed crushing plant. Do you know where that was, Mr. Speaker? In Windsor, Ontario. What did they crush? American corn and soybeans. There went diversification in western Canada down the drain. I do not think there are more than two or three oilseed crushing plants left in existence-
There are six.

Out of one dozen half of them have gone belly up.
Unless our geography and our industrial strategy is taken into account, this Bill will not accomplish what is the Government's objective, an objective with which we all agree. That means that under the industrial strategy we will have to discriminate in favour of a region such as western Canada, northern or Atlantic Canada which could well mean less growth, or a bit of a standstill in growth, in the golden triangle from Quebec to Windsor.
Western Economic Diversification Act
I put this question. Why do we want Toronto or Montreal to get any bigger? What for? Glorified ant hills is what they are. Why would one want to establish another manufacturing plant in that part of the country? As far as I am concerned Toronto needs another manufacturing plant like it needs a hole in the head. We have unemployed people in northern Ontario and northern Quebec. There are pockets of unemployment in different parts of the country. With an industrial strategy that is workable and meaningful, those are the places to which development would be directed.
I received a letter this morning from a manufacturer of wood products in British Columbia. He has offices in Vancouver and Rossland. I understand that he ships about 1,500 to
2,000	carloads of plywood every year. One could call that some amount of diversification. There is an application before the National Transportation Agency to abandon the whole railway line on which he ships his product. It is the boundary subdivision, 100 miles of track running through Castlegar. While we are debating this Bill, this nonsense in the House, there is a business that has been in operation for many years, a very reputable business which produces a good product, which is losing that railway line. This means that it is finished.
What are we doing? We are sitting back and letting the two national railways go through the process of abandoning a total of 15,000 miles of railway tracks in the country over the next five years. Why would one want to locate a processing plant or a manufacturing plant somewhere out West or somewhere in Atlantic Canada? What for, when one has to resort to putting the product manufactured on overcrowded highways at higher costs while one is still as far away from the markets as was one before? Why would one bother? What incentive is there to diversify in the West or in Atlantic Canada? There is not any. Our market is not big enough.
I return to my main point. There must be an industrial strategy. It has been done in other places. It reminds me of the story of the rooster which went out for a walk one morning. Egg production had gone down in the hen house and the farmer was about ready to butcher all the chickens. The rooster was pretty worried about it because he was going to get the axe as well. So he went out for a walk one morning and happened to get into the zoo. He came across an ostrich nest in which there were some ostrich eggs. He ran back to the chicken coop and rounded up all the hens and took them over to the ostrich nest. He said: "Look girls, I am not complaining but just look at what they are doing in other places". That is what we need to be doing. I am not suggesting that we copy what other countries have done word for word or line for line, but we need to adopt an industrial strategy meant for Canada that suits our requirements. It must fit in with our geography and climate. Darn it all, out West and in Atlantic Canada we can produce things just as good as anybody else anywhere else in the country if we are just given a fair chance to do so. This legislation does not set up that fair chance.
People talk about a level playing field, whether it be with respect to free trade or anything else. It is all very well to have

May 10, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
a playing field that is level, although I have never seen a level one yet. You will know, Mr. Speaker, that even a football field is not level. When we talk about level playing fields, that is fine, but when the other guy has the ball on our 10 yard line, then that ain't very level, is it? That illustrates what happens when something is being produced in western Canada in competition with the same thing in central Canada or in the United States. They have the ball on our 10-yard line. That is the name of the game. That might mean not only allocating where industry goes, agreeing where industry goes and allocating the area. It will mean a greater number of transportation subsidies. They can be called "subsidies" or transportation incentives, I do not care what name is put on it. If the Americans do not like it, tough cookie.
South of my province the States of North Dakota, South Dakota, and Montana are economic deserts. They have the same problem that we do. The distance that they are from their markets means that industry in those three states is minimal, if in existence at all. There the free market forces are allowed to continually be in play. That is not the Canadian way. That is not the way things have been done in Canada since before Sir John A. Macdonald.
If there was anything recognized by our forefathers and the people in Parliament in 1867 and thereafter, it was if the whole nation is going to be developed and kept together, some type of an equity of opportunity had to be built into our laws, transportation, and in government programs of various types. It is a fact of life in a northern nation like ours.
Again, Sir, I do not want to be partisan, because it will not matter what political Party is in power. Unless it is done in that manner, this Bill and others like it will not work. They are doomed to failure. We have gone through this before. Over the years we have had special agencies, special legislation, and special programs up to here. They last a year, or two, or three, and then die a deserving unnatural death.
I hope the Government will take into account what we in the Opposition, certainly my colleagues and I in the New Democratic Party, have had to say on this issue. We have tried to say those things in a positive and constructive manner to urge upon the Government to do it differently than we did it before. Let us not repeat the same mistakes and messes that were made before. We will all be happy about that. We will all make western Canada and Atlantic Canada much better places in which to live.

That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should give consideration to the report of the Special Joint Committee on Senate Reform,
presented to the House during the second session of the Thirty-Second
Parliament.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak this afternoon on Motion No. 84. Certainly, the issue of Senate reform has been something that this country has looked at and dealt with for a great many years. Very little over that time has in fact changed. However, I believe there has been enough discussion to suggest the current situation is unsatisfactory and is in need of change. There are those, I suppose, with views from all across the political spectrum. Some are opposed to the Senate and feel it should be abolished. I think members of the New Democratic Party hold that view. There are others who have studied this issue through the years and have come up with a variety of proposals for change to the Senate. The election of the Senate is only a first step.
In looking over the recent history, and I say "recent" in the perspective of this country, in the last 20 years there have been a variety of reports and studies, starting in 1969. The federal Government White Paper proposed a new Senate with half of the Senators appointed by the provinces and the other half by the federal Government. In 1972, a Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on the Constitution recommended increasing the number of western Senators and reducing the power of the Senate to a suspense of veto.
A 1975 constitutional amendment awards one Senate seat each to the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, bringing the total to 104 Senators. In 1978, Bill C-60 proposed replacing the Senate with a House of Federation, with the provinces and the federal Government each appointing half the members based on proportional representation. In 1979 the Supreme
Senate Reform
Court ruled that the proposals represent a constitutional amendment and would, therefore, require the approval of provincial legislatures as well as the federal Parliament.
The Canada West Foundation recommended replacing the Senate with a House of Provinces. British Columbia, the Ontario Advisory Committee on Confederation and the Canadian Bar Association also submitted reform proposals. In 1979 the Pepin-Roberts Task Force on Canadian Unity proposed replacing the Senate with a provincially appointed Council of Federation. In 1980, the federal and provincial Ministers responsible for constitutional matters discussed a new Upper House involving the provinces with no resolution. The report of the Standing Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs entitled "Certain Aspects on the Canadian Constitution" affirms the need for a nominated and substantially reformed Senate.
The Quebec Liberal Party's base paper entitled "A new Canadian Federation" proposed replacing the Senate with a federal council composed of provincial Government delegates. Again in 1981, the Canada West Foundation supported direct election of Senators based on single province-wide constituencies. In 1982, the Constitution Act provided for a six-months suspensory veto for the Senate with respect to constitutional amendment. Alberta also recommended provincial appointment of Senators, the Senate debates, the election of Senators by the people.
In 1983 a Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Senate reform starts work in April. The Business Council on National Issues supports election of Senators. The final report, the one we are discussing today, the report of the Special Joint Committee on Senate reform, was tabled in January of 1984. A lot of work went into the tabling of the Joint Committee on Senate Reform. I think those who have read it will agree there are areas in that report that were certainly well worthy of consideration and study at the time and have merit in following up on some of the recommendations that have been made.
What kind of elected Senate would serve Canada's system of responsible Government? The Senate, I think, should have significant powers but should not be able to undermine Canada's well tried system of responsible Government. Senators should have a significant degree of independence of Party which would enable them to speak on local and regional issues without adhering to Party policy.
We should consider the original purpose of the Senate, and perhaps we tend to get away from this when we are looking at suggested changes. The Senate was created in 1867 to fill not one but two major roles in the new federation. One was to protect and represent, so far as legislation was concerned, what Sir John A. Macdonald termed "sectional interests". This included those peculiar to a region or linguistic or religious groups. The other major role was to help political stability by acting as a counterweight to the elected House of Commons. These two rules were carried out by the exercise of sober

May 10, 1988
Senate Reform
second thought in review of legislation emanating from the Lower House, the House that drew its mandate from elections based on population, although in those days the franchise was restricted.
Criticisms have been directed at the Senate for a number of years, probably more so in the last few years, and again in the last several months, where most of us in our constituencies have been reminded of some of the Bills which have been in the Senate for some time and the role being played by those in the Senate.
I suppose the appointment of Senators has to be a difficult issue for any Prime Minister to face. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be taking part in the debate this afternoon on the motion by the Hon. Member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Porter). The question of Senate reform and the future of that institution is both timely and important. With passage of the Constitutional Accord, Senate reform will be the priority item in future federal-provincial negotiations. This fact should be welcomed by all Members of this House.
With the adoption of an amending formula requiring the consent of the federal Government and all provinces, the Accord, in the words of the Special Joint Committee, will assure that provinces such as Alberta, which feel strongly about Senate reform, cannot be forced to accept a Senate reform package that does not live up to their expectations. Despite this, there has been some talk by opponents of the Accord who would have us believe that future Senate reform will be impossible as a result of the change to the amending formula. This charge must be challenged and I propose to address this accusation in my remarks today.
Under the changes to the amending formula in the Accord no province is singled out for special status. The Accord ensures full consensus on fundamental changes affecting the federation, including Senate reform, an item now guaranteed to be on the agenda for future constitutional talks. Surely it is reasonable that there be a strong consensus on a reformed Senate. How can it be otherwise? Surely no one can seriously suggest that a future reformed Senate be imposed on provinces such as British Columbia or Alberta as it could be under the present formula when those provinces have a particular and long-standing concern with this issue.
Critics of the Accord, including some members of the Opposition, have suggested that we should maintain the old 70-50 rule for changes to the Senate on the grounds that reform will be more easy to achieve. I want to emphasize that the unanimity requirement does not spell the end of Senate reform. It reflects the principle of equality of the provinces, unlike the procedure for Senate reform adopted in 1982.
Unanimity was achieved on the constitutional amendments of 1940, 1951, 1960, and 1964, as well as on the complex set of issues in the Meech Lake Accord. Unanimity is already required for certain important matters of concern to the country as a whole, such as the composition of the Supreme Court and changes to the amending formula itself. Most amendments will still proceed with the support of seven provinces representing 50 per cent of the population. As for additional matters on which unanimity will be required, the proposed amendment will guarantee each province a say where
May 10, 1988

changes to key national institutions and the composition of the federation are considered.
The adoption of the Accord will allow Governments to proceed to address a range of issues with all provinces as full participants. The Accord guarantees annual First Ministers' Conferences on the Constitution, and two items, Senate reform and roles and responsibility in relation to fisheries, have been placed on the agenda for these conferences. Public discussion and debate in Parliament and the legislative assemblies will help Governments assess how they might consider other constitutional issues.
On the question of unanimity I would like to quote Peter Meekison, an expert on Canadian federalism and a long-time constitutional negotiator for the Alberta Government. He told the special joint committee that: "Senate reform is no more difficult under the proposed change than it is under the existing formula in that-it is very difficult for a province to cast a veto. The natural tendency-is to try to find a compromise." Many of the same factors that led to unanimity at Meech Lake will play a part in the process of Senate reform.
The Canadian Senate was originally charged with the responsibility for protecting what Sir John A. Macdonald called "sectional interests". The establishment of this institution was a critical part of the Confederation agreement. The Senate was to offset representation by population in the House of Commons. There are two important reasons why the Senate has been unable to protect regional interests adequately. First, non-elected Senators are not considered to be legitimate regional or provincial voices in Parliament. Second, the distribution of Senate seats gives a near majority to the two most populous provinces. It does not, therefore, provide an adequate means to temper the expression of majority will in the House of Commons. To the suggestion that the Accord will make Senate reform more difficult, Senator Lowell Murray said in a speech at a national conference on Senate reform last week in Edmonton that:
1 would simply reply that without Quebec's return to the constitutional table, Senate reform is impossible. Moreover, if the Senate is to become a vital national institution, we have to go about reforming it in the right way. We must recognize the vital interest that all provinces have in such national institutions, we must respect the principle of the equality of the provinces, and the need to secure consensus before making fundamental changes.
The interim procedure agreed upon for Senate appointments is not intended to be permanent. Rather, the proposed amendment explicitly states it is to apply "until an amendment to the Constitution of Canada is made in relation to the Senate." The unanimity rule will protect each province against an amendment to national institutions unacceptable to that province. Therefore, unanimity is as much a source of protection as it is a potential hurdle.
The Accord reinforces the federal character of the Senate by acknowledging the legitimate role played by the provinces in the choice of candidates who must nevertheless have the approval of the federal Government, which continues to make
Senate Reform
the appointments. As Senator Murray said in the other place on March 31:
We have had enough of isolating provinces in constitutional processes. We have had enough of running roughshod over concerns that are vital to a province's interest.
I could not agree more. I would also like to refer to an address given to the Institute of Island Studies on April 11 by Premier Ghiz of Prince Edward Island. He noted that:
Pending Senate reform, all appointments are made from lists supplied by the provinces. In an historical context-this provision is quite a reasonable one and in no way signals a lessening of the executive power of the central government.
I would conclude my remarks by saying that for future Senate reform to succeed, all parts of Canada must be assured that the Senate speaks in a particular way for their own specific interests. I personally feel strongly that Senate reform is necessary and no less possible with the adoption of the Meech Lake Accord. However, I cannot and will not at this time go on record as being in favour of an elected Senate.
This Government, under the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), is dedicated to seeking agreement on a reformed Senate that will ensure regional interests figure more prominently in national decision-making. There is strong support for Senate reform among the provinces and a desire to work together with the Government of Canada toward that end. The result will be a balanced national Government within a strong federation.
The skeptics and pessimists were proven wrong last June when they said Quebec could not be brought into the constitutional fold. I have no doubt they will be proven wrong again on the subject of Senate reform.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to take part in this debate on the motion of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Porter). The motion before the House calls upon the Government to give special consideration to the 1984 report of the Special Joint Committee on Senate Reform.
This is a most timely debate, especially for those of us from Alberta. It is now just over a year since the signing of the Meech Lake Accord on April 30, 1987. The Accord represents the beginning of a new era in Canadian federalism. As well as bringing Quebec into the constitutional family, the Accord provides new constitutional and institutional arrangements to
Senate Reform
encourage closer, more harmonious relations between the federal and provincial governments.
One of the most significant aspects of the Accord is its commitment to further constitutional reform and to Senate reform in particular. It is to this issue specifically that I address my comments this afternoon.
As Hon. Members will be aware, the constitutional Accord of June 3, 1987, provides for an entrenched second round of discussions aimed at fostering further constitutional development. In particular, the Accord requires the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to convene a First Ministers' Conference on the Constitution at least once a year once the Meech Lake amendments have been proclaimed. Among the items on the agenda for these conferences will be Senate reform. This will include the role and functions of the Senate; the powers of the Senate; the method of selecting Senators; representation in the Senate.
As a result of a change in the amending formula, the consent of all provinces will be required for amendments to these matters. In future, each province will have an equal say on this vital issue. This contrasts with the present arrangement which grants a veto to Ontario and Quebec acting together, but not to any other two provinces acting together.
Finally, as a demonstration of the Prime Minister's good faith and commitment, the Accord provides that until constitutional amendments on the Senate are achieved, the federal Government will appoint Senators from among candidates proposed by provincial Governments and who are acceptable to the federal Government. The provinces thus will have a real say on appointments to the Senate until more comprehensive reform is achieved.
Contrary to what some critics of the Accord have suggested, the Accord provides for the full and open discussion that I believe all aspects of Senate reform deserve. It assures that all the major points that need to be addressed must be considered at annual First Ministers' Conferences.
Senate reform has been the subject of many studies and reports over the years. The report of the Special Joint Committee on Senate Reform was an important and useful contribution to this ongoing question. It recommended that the Senate be directly elected in order to "strengthen the authority of Parliament to speak and act on behalf of Canadians in all parts of the country".
The Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) was a distinguished member of the Special Joint Committee which tabled its report in January, 1984. The report called for a directly elected Senate, with a weighted representation of seats to increase regional representation. Senators would be elected for a single nine-year term, with one-third of the Senators elected every three years. The Senate would have a 120-day suspensive veto over ordinary legislation, and ratification authority over Order in Council appointments to federal agencies with important regional implications.

May 10, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
Other reports may differ on the precise composition and powers of a reformed Senate. I think it is safe to say, however, that there is a strong feeling that an appointed Senate no longer meets the needs of the Canadian federation, especially in the area of regional representation.
I believe that we simply can no longer tolerate a situation in which an appointed, non-accountable body such as the present Senate acts to frustrate the will of the democratically elected House of Commons. We have seen the Senate take it upon itself to delay several important pieces of legislation over the course of this Parliament. These include Bills on immigration and refugees, drug patent protection, and copyright protection. That is clearly unacceptable in a modern, democratic society.
At the present time the Senate speaks for no one but itself and the interests of the majority party in that chamber. In doing so, the Senate has only managed to raise public awareness of the inadequacies of the Senate and the need for fundamental reform. Some critics have suggested that passage of the Accord should be made contingent upon Senate reform. There has been an agreement since August, 1986, that Senate reform is a second round issue. The terms of the Meech Lake Accord fully reflect the distinction that the First Ministers made between the Quebec round and the second round.
The requirement for unanimity has raised a fear in some quarters that Senate reform will be impossible. Senate reform is only impossible as long as Quebec is not at the table. Would it be healthy for confederation if a province were to have its representation on the Senate reduced without its consent? No. That sort of thinking belongs in the past.
The Prime Minister has said he will table a Senate reform proposal on behalf of the federal Government at the initial Conference of the First Ministers following ratification of the Accord. The Prime Minister also indicated in the House on August 26, 1987, that Parliament will have a role in paving the way for the discussion of Senate reform at that Conference.
As a further indication of the seriousness with which the Government approaches the question of Senate reform, I would refer Hon. Members to an excellent speech delivered last week by the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations, Senator Lowell Murray. In his May 5 address before the National Conference on Senate Reform at the University of Alberta, the Hon. Senator said:
I speak for the Prime Minister and all my Cabinet colleagues in saying that we know the importance that is attached to Senate reform by Canadians- especially those who live in Western Canada-and that we are convinced of its importance in the future of our country.
Those who support a directly elected Senate can also take encouragement, because as Senator Murray went on to say:
When the present round is complete, the Prime Minister has made clear that the Government of Canada will put forward a proposal for Senate reform. While the basic elements of the Government's position are emerging-one thing, however, is clear.
If the vitality of our democratic institutions is to be strengthened, the Senate should be elected. A second thing is also clear: we should ensure the Senate has
the means to act effectively while preserving the accountability of the
government to the House of Commons within our system.
In conclusion, I would like to express my agreement with Senator Murray that Senate reform is a national constitutional issue and the Senate is potentially a key national institution. This Government has consistently demonstrated its ongoing commitment to national reconciliation, including institutional reform.
I believe the Constitutional Accord outlines the best way to proceed on Senate reform. On this issue, as on several others, the Accord charts the right path to the future, a path that will encourage full federal-provincial collaboration as we consider changes to the key federal institutions and as we carry on the day-to-day business of the federation.

HER MAJESTY QUEEN BEATRIX OF THE NETHERLANDS to

HOUSE OF COMMONS CHAMBER, OTTAWA on

Her Majesty was welcomed by the Right Honourable Brian Mulroney, Prime Minister of Canada, and thanked by the Honourable Guy Charbonneau, Speaker of the Senate and the Honourable John A. Fraser, Speaker of the House of Commons.

speakeroldname: Hon. John A. Fraser (Speaker of the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The Right Honourable the Prime Minister.

Your Majesty, Your Royal Highness, chers collegues, Honourable Senators:
It is a great honour for me to welcome you here today. On behalf of the Canadian Government, please allow me again to extend, Your Majesty and Your Royal Highness, our warmest welcome to Canada and especially to Ottawa. May I say it in a special way. When you are here in the House of Commons, Your Majesty, and in Ottawa, you are back home.
Hear, hear!

In a special sense I say, "Welcome home, bienvenue chez vous".
The relationships that exist between our two nations are in many ways unique. They are based first on immigration, which binds us together with family ties. Nearly a million Canadians pride themselves on their Dutch ancestry, and their contribution to Canada has been absolutely magnificent. There is the legacy of valour of the Second World War, during which our soldiers, our young men and women, fought for the freedom of your country.
I must pay special homage to the Members of Parliament, both past and present, who participated in the liberation of the Netherlands, including our very distinguished Minister of Veterans Affairs, the Honourable George Hees, who is with us here, Your Majesty, today.

Hear, hear!
[DOT] (mo)

He says, Your Majesty, that he entered the Canadian Forces as a boy of nine!
This afternoon, Your Majesty and Your Royal Highness will be inaugurating "The Sweetest Spring", an exhibition of art and artifacts at the Canadian War Museum. This exhibit, jointly mounted by the Canadian War Museum and the Royal Netherlands Army Museum, underlines our close ties and reinforces our common values.
[ Translation]
Our nations cherish the same important ideals of peace, justice and freedom. The presence of your family in Ottawa during the dark days of World War II formed the basis for a direct affinity between members of your family and Canada, and for a deep affection between Canadians and you yourself.

I know, Your Majesty, that you have fond memories of Stornoway, where you resided temporarily in Ottawa. I also have fond memories of Stornoway, where I resided temporarily in Ottawa. In fact, Your Majesty, all Leaders of the Opposition in Canada have come to regard this gracious home as essentially a temporary residence.
The splendid Dutch tulips, now in bloom on Parliament Hill and throughout our capital, are an enduring legacy of your family's wartime stay in Canada. This generous gift from Queen Juliana to the people of Canada is a unique tribute and one which all Canadians value, particularly at this time of year. When Princess Margriet was born here, the colours of the Netherlands were raised above these Parliament Buildings, celebrating the unprecedented event of a member of a reigning European Royal Family being born on North American soil.
Today this rich heritage has produced a wealth of political, economic, social, and trade relationships.

Your visit to Canada reaffirms the importance of our relations with the European Economic Community, with Western Europe and especially with the Netherlands. The history and the future of Western Europe are closely linked with our history and our future. Together we have formed an association as fruitful as it is diversified, based on political, economic and cultural ties, an unshakeable faith in democracy and an ardent desire to preserve our freedom.
The Netherlands have played a fundamental role in the development of Western civilization. To Canadians, Your Majesty, your country has always been synonymous with social justice and respect for human rights.
May 10, 1988



I am pleased to note that our dialogue in this area has been active and fruitful. I would like to underline, Your Majesty, the fact that we share similar views on major international issues should come as a surprise to no one. Our countries are committed members of the international community with similar political, economic, and trade objectives. Most of all, Your Majesty, our countries and our peoples are friends- friends who share values and traditions, friends who espouse the same principles, and whose children dream the same dreams.
On behalf of the Government of the people of Canada, I welcome you to Canada and, through you, extend our warmest greetings to the people of the Netherlands.
Your Majesty, may I ask you at this special and affectionate moment of home-coming to speak now to the Parliament and to all of the people of Canada.

Hear, hear!
Her Majesty Queen Beatrix of the Netherlands: Mr. Speaker, ladies and gentlemen, our meeting with the Canadian Parliament is taking place in the year in which we are commemorating the Glorious Revolution of 1688, which placed Dutch Stadholder William III together with his wife, Mary Stuart II on the throne of England.
The Glorious Revolution stands as a landmark in the development of British parliamentary democracy. By virtue of the Bill of Rights then presented to William of Orange and his wife before they ascended the throne, Britain's Parliament regained its traditional significance. The Bill of Rights reasserted that the Sovereign could only rule with the consent of the representatives of his subjects. To many peoples in the seventeenth century that was a revolutionary principle; the people of the Netherlands, however, had adopted the principle a century earlier. The subsequent political development of both the United Kingdom and the British Commonwealth was conditioned by the principle of consent. In a few weeks, on the twentieth of July, the British House of Commons, the mother of all parliaments, will commemorate the events of 1688. It is pleasing to know that delegations from the Canadian and Netherlands parliaments will attend the ceremony.
In Canada in 1839 Lord Durham laid the foundations for a democratic form of government in his "Report on the Affairs of British North America". On the basis of the "responsible government" principle he entrusted the government of the colony to the colonists themselves. The policy of placing the responsibility for government with the people was thereby extended to Canada.
To our countries this form of responsibility has long ceased to be a matter of doubt or debate. In fact, we should now attach to the term "responsible government", the essence of the Durham report, a different, far deeper significance. Since then our dealings have become more international, our present
more linked to the future. Besides to their own citizens, to whom governments are quite naturally answerable, they are therefore feeling increasingly answerable to those with whom we share the world and to generations as yet unborn. This is the new signification of "responsible government".
The peoples of countries such as Canada and the Netherlands are particularly conscious of their common destiny with the other inhabitants of our globe. National decisions are increasingly making themselves felt far beyond frontiers. Governments are also increasingly being confronted with tasks they can no longer perform alone.
An international task for Canada was implicit in the three basic principles, namely, Peace, order and Good Government, of the Constitution Act, 1867. The maintenance of "Order" is a function that a government could perform alone, but not the maintenance of "Peace". By definition, therefore, "Good Government" can imply nothing but to govern in collaboration with other countries.
Canadians have long been aware of the fact that their country is a member of a global community. It was this realization that led to Canada's willingness to make sacrifices in the great conflicts of this century. Canada made an impressive contribution to the victory of the Allies in World War 1. She then played a prominent role as an active member of the League of Nations. Canadian participation in World War II was further evidence of her sense of international solidarity, which was of incalculable moment, particularly to the Netherlands. Much of Holland was liberated by Canadian soldiers, all of whom, exactly like their fathers, had crossed the Atlantic Ocean as volunteers to destroy a power and an ideology that posed a mortal threat to our common civilization. A few days ago, on the 4th and 5th of May, Holland gratefully commemorated the 1945 liberation and, as in every year, flowers were laid on the graves of members of the Canadian Forces who found their last resting place in our country.
After our common struggle in that war, our equally common conviction that democratic states should together safeguard their security found expression in new forms of co-operation among allies. Canada and the Netherlands have already been members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization for 40 years. Both countries have from the outset regarded NATO as an organization that embraces more than mere common military defence. Article II of the treaty by which NATO was established speaks of the parties strengthening their free institutions, their democratic institutions, encouraging economic collaboration and creating a true Atlantic community. It is significant that this section was called "the Canadian Article".
A feeling of responsibility for the destiny of the world in general is also evident from the two countries' active participation in the work of the United Nations. An appeal to Canada for peace-keeping operations has never been in vain. Canada

May 10, 1988
and the Netherlands are also co-members of many other international institutions. Not only do their representatives meet each other there, they often defend the same points of view. A noteworthy unanimity between two countries here bridges the difference that separates them. Countries like Canada and Holland can make a valuable contribution, especially internationally, in the form of ideas, initiatives and mediation. Backed by the confidence they have gradually managed to inspire in the world, the very countries that are not among the superpowers may thus play a sometimes disproportionately important role.
One of the main aims of our two countries is the global promotion of the international rule of law. This is where we touch the heart of our responsibility for relations in today's world, a world teeming with problems. I will name only one of them: the lagging behind of what we call the Third World, that extensive area in which equitable relations leave a great deal to be desired and where the international rule of law is least in evidence. The duty not to acquiesce in that lag in development is implicit in "responsible government". Canada and the Netherlands give high priority to aid for the Third World and to economic co-operation with Third World countries. Our two nations have for years done much in this area, both to alleviate poverty directly and to render assistance in the longer term, to help people to help themselves. It was no mere chance that the first compendious United Nations report on Third World problems was drawn up by a commission chaired by Lester Pearson.
But "responsible government" in the field of development co-operation may not stop at emergency aid and charity. Neither is the transfer of capital and know-how sufficient. The opening of our markets is, economically and psychologically, just as important. That is the only way in which we can make a real contribution toward growth in the countries themselves. Indeed, it is disturbing that some developed countries are again considering protectionist measures. Protectionism is ultimately bad for everyone, but the poor countries are the victims; they are the first and the worst affected. By giving in to the inclination to protect ourselves we cause multiple damage, we hamper economic growth and increase injustice in the world. An open economy is both a Canadian and a Dutch tradition. It is pre-eminently a tradition we may not abandon.

Mr. Speaker, Lord Durham's compelling plea for "responsible government" alluded to responsibility towards citizens. The passage of time and social developments have given the term a new signification. As distances shrank and the interdependence of countries severally increased, we became ever more conscious of our responsibility towards all those who with us populate the world. This realization goes very deep in Canada and the Netherlands.
Moreover, the recent past has given the term "responsible government" a new dimension, our answerability for the
future, the obligation to leave behind for our children a world fit to live in.
Fifteen years ago the Club of Rome in its first report gave an urgent warning. As we see it now, the warning was perhaps not urgent enough. Not only is our highly developed society threatened by a future shortage of raw materials, but the very level of development we have already reached holds treats to our well-being, to say nothing of the hazards that loom if the creation of further opulence goes on at the same hectic pace.
It is essential that environmental research conducive to the adoption of rational measures be stepped up and that the efficacy of such research be increased through international co-operation. Preventive intervention is imperative in view of the irreversibility of certain processes that harm the environment. It is true that the very technical knowledge that threatens our future will often enable us to redress the damage done, but we only really control technology if we employ it to prevent damage. Only the courage to take unpopular measures now will safeguard the future for coming generations. The requirement that the quality of the heritage we have received and that we in turn shall have to hand on to posterity may not be impaired is not yet universally realized. Essential, fundamental alterations in our pattern of behaviour are overdue. The close attention of parliament and environment-conscious citizens is a requisite, a stimulus and a guarantee of an effective policy in this area. Politicians and industrialists must join forces and find the answers.
Illustrative of Canada's attitude is that the major United Nations conference on the ozone layer was held in Montreal last year, and that now Canada is again busy preparing a conference on "controlled development" as a follow-up of the Brundtland report.
There have been a number of successes in environmental protection, both national and international. A bolder approach at global level that takes the interconnection of matters concerning food supplies, the generation of power, development aid and the environment into account, is however required. The parallel Canadian and Dutch views on these problems and the approach to them invite a greater common advance in international planning.
In a bilateral context, environmental technology is one of the important fields in which Canada and Holland exchange know-how and experience. A Memorandum of Understanding between our governments on the subject was signed yesterday; similar memoranda with the governments of Ontario and Quebec are to be concluded shortly.
Mr. Speaker, Members of the House and the Senate, since the first parliament was set up, the elected representatives have fulfilled the mandate entrusted to them by the people. In our times, parliamentarians have been given another, double mandate: one by those with whom we live on this globe and
May 10, 1988

one by generations as yet unborn. The commitment to "responsible government", which cabinets and parliaments must honour has thereby been made much more onerous a task, and it demands courage to commit oneself wholly to this objective.
The term we must now have in mind is moreover far longer than the life of a parliament. The sense of responsibility for others and for the future is nevertheless deeply rooted in this legislative body. It was in this parliament, where I am your guest today, that political democracy was established in Canada in the 19th century. It is heartening to note that the members of today's assembly realize that they are now the guardians of a responsible democracy. Thank you.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Guy Charbonneau (Speaker of the Senate):
speechtext:
Your Majesty, Your Royal Highness, on behalf of the Senate I want to thank you most heartily for your remarks, which were a vivid testimony to the quality and vigour that characterize our bilateral relations, and to the importance of those relations.
Nor can I resist commenting on how very rare it is to receive within these walls the sovereign of a friendly and allied power who can point to a childhood spent, in part, in Canada's capital. It gives us, I think, an additional reason for our pleasure in welcoming you today to the Parliament of Canada. It is one of the distinguishing features of the links that bind our two countries. Our long tradition of working together to preserve the values that are dear to us reinforces the significance of the personal link, which has been extended in the most natural way by the many other family ties between Canada and the Netherlands.
[ Translation]
Your profound statements come as no surprise to students of the political writings of your great philosopher, Spinoza. Your reign as we have seen, continues the admirable example of your predecessors who were mindful of the role Spinoza urged governing authorities to play when he stated, and this was in the seventeenth century, that the rights of the individual took precedence over the authority of the State. Need I recall in your presence his warning that the State that denied this principle would be mere power and be vanquished by power?
It is indeed very fitting to say in this Chamber that you have evoked the great humanist tradition that brought us the principle of intellectual freedom. We understand why Descartes, attracted by the tolerance and love of freedom of your people, spent twenty years in Holland, and why Pascal admired the dialectics of your philosphers. The tradition continues today, at a time when your thinkers have spearheaded the movement for religious reform throughout the world, taking the calculated risk of bringing about a moral crisis.

The friendship between our two countries is consolidated by the significant commercial exchanges between us. Renowned
for their technological innovations and business sense, the Dutch are valued partners for dynamic, technologically advanced, and resource rich countries like Canada. Dutch investments in this country are already quite substantial and the possibility of more joint ventures and increased trade can only fortify our commercial relations.
Our cultural ties are also especially important for Canadians of Dutch origin who want to maintain their links with the Netherlands, but all Canadians cherish the spirit of friendship and co-operation which permeates our relations with your country. Our economic contacts, official visits, and the significant flow of tourists in both directions illustrate the wish of our citizens not only to retain our special ties, but also to nurture them for our mutual benefit.
Your Majesty, your visit to Canada will give you the opportunity to witness the vitality of our young country, but I have no doubt that the warmth of our feelings toward the Dutch nation will also become evident. I trust your trip will be a pleasant one and that it will provide you with more fond memories of Canada.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Your Majesty, Your Royal Highness-

Speaking on behalf of my colleagues in the House of Commons and of other honoured guests present in this Chamber, I wish to thank you for your most cordial speech. Canadians of Dutch descent have played a major role in many areas of Canadian society.

There have been people from your country, Your Majesty, in Canada from our earliest days. Their continuing presence explains why there is a certain resemblance between our two countries. We are convinced that this visit by Your Majesty and Your Royal Highness will help to reinforce those similarities and enable us to extend our co-operation along a number of promising avenues, taking as our starting point our already thriving relationship. Your profound appreciation of the need for international co-operation, especially in regard to our environment, has been most certainly noted in this Chamber today.
I would like to take this opportunity, presented by your presence within these walls, to ask you to convey the best wishes of the Canadian House of Commons to the people of your country and to assure them of our friendship. To you, Your Majesty, and Your Royal Highness, you will always be home in our country. God bless you.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
